planting.note: Plant the large corm in rich, well-drained, humus-heavy potting mix in bright, warm, humid conditions; grown almost exclusively in large containers, conservatories, or botanical garden collections due to its eventual enormous size and the many years required to reach flowering maturity.

directions: Grow in rich, humus-heavy, well-drained soil in warm, humid, bright but filtered light, mimicking the understory conditions of its native Sumatran rainforest. The titan arum is world-famous as the corpse flower, producing the largest unbranched inflorescence of any plant on Earth, occasionally reaching eight to ten feet tall, which emits an overpowering smell of rotting flesh for the roughly 24 to 48 hours it is open in order to attract carrion beetles and flies as pollinators. Between blooms the corm produces a single enormous, tree-like compound leaf on a mottled stalk that can itself reach 15 to 20 feet, storing energy in the corm, which can eventually weigh over 100 pounds. It typically takes seven to ten years or more from seed or offset before a corm is large enough to flower for the first time, and blooming events remain rare and celebrated even in dedicated botanical garden collections. This is a specialist plant requiring significant space, warmth, and years of patient care rather than a typical home garden subject.

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors. Silver Bay tolerates lower light better than most other silver-patterned aglaonema cultivars.

directions: Plant in low to bright indirect light — no direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, evenly moist potting mix. Silver Bay produces broad, upright leaves in silvery-grey-green with darker green margins and speckling, a cooler, more muted color scheme than the warmer reds or bright whites of other popular aglaonema cultivars, giving it a calm, sophisticated look that pairs well in mixed plantings without competing for attention. It is an easygoing, slow-growing plant that tolerates missed waterings and average indoor humidity far better than most tropical foliage plants, and it is among the more shade-tolerant aglaonema cultivars, holding good color even in dimmer interior corners. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings, avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, and in zone 9 it can spend the warm season on a shaded porch before returning indoors well ahead of frost.

common_name: Emerald Bay Aglaonema (Dark Green Silver-Patterned Chinese Evergreen)

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors. Emerald Bay is among the more shade-tolerant aglaonema cultivars since it carries less light-dependent pale variegation than pink or white cultivars.

directions: Plant in low to bright indirect light — no direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, evenly moist potting mix. Emerald Bay carries deep, glossy green leaves overlaid with an irregular pattern of lighter silver-green blotching that follows the leaf veins, a classic and subtle patterning that reads as elegant and understated rather than boldly colorful, and its predominantly green coloring makes it more tolerant of low light than pink, red, or heavily white-variegated aglaonema cultivars. It is an easygoing, slow-growing plant that tolerates missed waterings and average indoor humidity far better than most tropical foliage plants, forming a dense, clumping rosette over time. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings, avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, and in zone 9 it can spend the warm season on a shaded porch before returning indoors well ahead of frost.
